Issued at 423 AM CDT Sun Aug 9 2026

A prolonged, convectively-active period is expected across the 
Midwest through much of this week as a muggy and unstable air 
mass stubbornly hovers over the region over the next several 
days. That said, confidence in forecast specifics regarding the
thunderstorm potential for any given day during this period is 
inherently low given the nature of this summertime air mass, the
involvement of subtle forcing mechanisms, and the influence of 
one convective cycle on the next and the subsequent domino 
effects that follow.

First thing's first, though. Clear skies and calm/light winds 
have allow for some fog develop in our area early this morning,
mainly focused outside of the Chicago and Rockford metro area. 
Thus far, it appears that any denser fog has remained patchy 
based on area webcams, but we'll continue to monitor the 
potential need for a targeted Dense Fog Advisory as the morning 
goes along.

Anyways, circling back to today's thunderstorm potential... 
There still appear to be two potential windows for thunderstorms
in our area today. The first window will be from around midday 
through this afternoon and will be tied to the convection that 
is ongoing to our west at this early hour in Iowa and eastern 
South Dakota. There was concern earlier that the storms eastern 
South Dakota could grow upscale into a mature, well-organized 
MCS that would plow through our area later today. While such a 
scenario isn't quite out of the equation just yet, the 
extensive, messy nature of the convection ongoing across Iowa 
does lend doubt to that scenario being realized. However, some 
loosely-organized conglomerate of the ongoing Iowa and South 
Dakota storms and/or any new convection that sprouts between or
just north of them will still likely drift towards our area, 
with the associated outflow likely to press eastward into 
forecast area later today. By the time this outflow arrives here
around the early afternoon, convective inhibition to 2000-3000 
J/kg of MLCAPE here will have largely been eroded, and new 
updrafts will be able to go up along it uninhibited. However, 
questions still remain regarding the strength of the attendant 
cold pool and the degree of convergence along this boundary, as 
the relative lack of synoptic-scale forcing support this 
afternoon will necessitate stronger lift at the surface for 
storms to develop and harness the full potential of the 
thermodynamic environment in place. The storms that do end up 
pulsing high enough this afternoon will be capable of producing
localized damaging winds and possibly a few instances of 1+" 
diameter hail.

The second window for storms in our area is expected to come 
late this afternoon into tonight as a low-level jet ramps up and
a shortwave trough passes by to our north. Note that it is 
possible that there may not be much of a break between these two
potential storm windows. The outflow boundary from the earlier 
convection will likely be laid out somewhere in or very near our
forecast area by this evening, and increasing isentropic ascent
atop this boundary will likely generate new convection along it
during this second thunderstorm window as long as the storms 
from earlier in the day don't end up being overly robust and 
extensive in coverage. How much instability will be available 
for these later storms to work with will depend on how strong
and widespread the earlier storms were, but deep-layer shear 
looks to be sufficiently strong to support rotating updrafts 
with any mature convection during this second thunderstorm
window. Damaging winds and hail will thus be possible with 
these storms, and a threat for tornadoes also couldn't be ruled 
out with any supercells that develop near the outflow boundary
if the boundary layer on the cool side of the outflow boundary 
manages to re-destabilize in time before nocturnal 
stabilization starts to set in. If the outflow boundary were to 
get laid out in a northwest-southeast orientation like some 
CAMs have been showing, then that would increase the likelihood 
of storms training over the same area. With the muggy air mass 
being conducive to torrential rainfall rates, this would raise 
concern for the threat for flash flooding tonight.

Regardless of how the storms in our area play out today and 
tonight, today's moist and unstable air mass will not budge much
going into tomorrow, so conditions on Monday will remain 
favorable for additional thunderstorms to develop in the region 
once again. Confidence in forecast specifics for Monday remains 
relatively low owing to there being some dependence on tonight's
convective footprint, but broadly speaking, most of the latest 
CAM guidance keeps our area devoid of thunderstorm activity 
during the daytime hours tomorrow due to a combination of 
capping and a lack of large-scale forcing mechanisms outside of
